endorsements.title: CHAI AI governance frameworks (playbooks)
endorsements.quote: Invest in end user education that emphasizes the limits of AI outputs and the staff obligation to verify AI outputs for the specific context.

endorsements.title: Collaborative and Cooperative Hospital "In-House" Medical Device Development and Implementation in the AI Age: The European Responsible AI Development (EURAID) Framework Compatible With European Values
endorsements.quote: With regard to content, it is important to define responsibilities within the company regarding who will take ownership of training the users in basic competencies of AI literacy.

commentary.bottom_line: No supplied study tests whether assigning explicit accountability for AI staff training, or documenting training requirements in policy, changes staff competence, verification behavior, or patient outcomes. Support for the recommendation rests on two expert sources, a CHAI governance playbook and the EURAID commentary, and neither reports empirical data.

perspectives.view: The evidence base contains zero studies testing the practice and zero studies documenting the hazard. The two endorsements are a framework and a commentary, which GRADE treats as expert opinion rather than evidence. Certainty therefore cannot be rated above no direct evidence, and the direction and size of any effect remain unknown.

No supplied study shows that training responsibilities actually fall between health systems and vendors, or that such gaps lead to unverified AI outputs reaching patients. The CHAI playbook links training to staff verifying outputs in context, but that link is asserted rather than measured in the material provided.

commentary.research_gap: Studies are needed that compare health systems or units with and without a named owner and written policy for AI training, measuring training completion, staff ability to recognize AI output limits, verification rates, and downstream errors. Descriptive work on how often vendor contracts leave training duties unassigned would also establish whether the targeted hazard occurs and how often.
commentary.underserved_note: No study tested the practice, so no evidence exists on whether it performs differently in Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy settings. Safety-net systems may have fewer staff to own training, and the effect of this recommendation in those settings is untested.
